paras: The kidnapping of Jesse Jones and Eugene Stroman was the night seizure, on July 22, 1920, of two Black farm hands near Wadesboro, Anson County, North Carolina, by three white men from Bamberg County, South Carolina, who carried them handcuffed across the state line. The planter W. D. Mayfield, who led the party, had accused the two of selling mortgaged property, and North Carolina's governor had refused to return them. The "Mayfield kidnapping case" became a two-month extradition contest between the governors and ended with guilty pleas and fines at Wadesboro.

Jones and Stroman had worked on Mayfield's farm near Denmark and in April 1920 left for the Zorn farm in Anson County. Mayfield charged that they had sold property under his chattel mortgage, and on April 21 Governor Cooper of South Carolina requisitioned them. Governor Bickett of North Carolina refused, according to The State because the papers seemed issued "for the collection of a debt."

Jones and Stroman swore that between 1 and 2 a.m. on July 22 a party led by J. F. Tice, a North Carolina constable, came to Jones's house posing as federal revenue officers. Jones said Tice, Mayfield and James Breedin drew revolvers, Mayfield handcuffed him, and, with a revolver at his neck, ordered him to call Stroman out or "I'll shoot your head off." Stroman was taken without his shoes and handcuffed to Jones.

With Mayfield's car stuck in the mud, Tice hired a Wadesboro driver, Earle Benton, who swore he carried the two men, handcuffed together, to Cheraw, where Mayfield and Henry B. Sandifer took them on to Bamberg. Both said they went because they feared being killed if they resisted. According to Sheriff W. S. Braswell of Anson County, they were tried at Denmark, found not guilty, and returned to North Carolina, where Jones swore out a kidnapping warrant.

Bickett requisitioned Mayfield, Breedin and Sandifer at the end of July, and Tice was arrested in North Carolina. At an August 7 hearing, J. A. Lockhart, for North Carolina, said he could prove impersonation of officers and forcible entry of a dwelling, a capital offense he did not intend to press. Cooper honored the requisition on September 6, saying many South Carolinians had urged him to refuse it.

Freed in Columbia on September 11, the three went voluntarily to Wadesboro on September 18 and pleaded guilty before Judge P. A. McElroy, saying they had not known they were breaking North Carolina law. Mayfield was fined $300 and Sandifer $150, judgment against Breedin was suspended, and Mayfield had to post $1,000 bond to show that the Bamberg cases against the farm hands were dismissed. Lockhart then announced federal charges for impersonating officers; no report of that prosecution appears in the coverage.

Coverage came almost entirely from Columbia dispatches in South Carolina papers such as the Sumter Watchman and Southron, the Bamberg Herald and the Lancaster News, with a wire item in the Montgomery Advertiser. They treated the case as an extradition contest, called Mayfield a "prominent planter" and "well-to-do," and called the victims "negro farm hands." They printed both sides' affidavits at length, and by late September a headline said the men had "Forcibly Arrested Negro Farm Hands" "Without Legal Process."

The only Black-press report found, in the Chicago Whip of August 14, ran as "Carolina Governors at Dagger Points." Its Raleigh dispatch named the abductors as white, counted "several colored men," blamed "South Carolina officials," and stressed the "tense and bitter feeling between the two Carolinas."

Mayfield swore that the two men "cheerfully accompanied" his party and denied posing as officers, using revolvers or handcuffs, though at trial he admitted they were armed. Jones and Stroman testified that they were handcuffed and taken against their will. Columbia dispatches differed on whether Cooper's revocation or a habeas corpus order freed the men, and a Newberry headline gave Mayfield's fine as $500.

reader.title: Kidnapping of Jesse Jones and Eugene Stroman
bases: A planter and two associates, with a North Carolina constable, seized at night and carried back across the state line two Black farm hands who had left his employ and whom he accused of selling mortgaged property and owing him money, after the North Carolina governor refused to return them as a debt matter (A2, A6, A14).

Many South Carolina reports, the victims' and the driver's affidavits, Mayfield's own affidavit and trial testimony, and the Chicago Whip agree that the three men took the two farm hands from Anson County to South Carolina, and the three pleaded guilty (A6, A7, A8, A17, A19); whether the men went by force is contested.

accounts.label: Jones and Stroman (affidavits and testimony)
accounts.gist: A party posing as revenue officers drew revolvers, handcuffed them in the night, threatened to shoot Jones, and carried them to South Carolina against their will; they went for fear of being killed.

accounts.label: Earle Benton (driver's affidavit)
accounts.gist: Tice hired his car about 4 a.m. and he carried Tice, Breedin and the two men, handcuffed together the whole way, to Cheraw.

accounts.label: Mayfield (affidavit and trial testimony)
accounts.gist: Told the men wished to return, he went for them; they cheerfully came along knowing a warrant awaited them; no officer impersonation, revolvers or handcuffs, though at trial he admitted the party was armed.

accounts.label: Sheriff Braswell
accounts.gist: The men were brought by rail to Denmark, tried and found not guilty, returned to North Carolina, and Jones swore out a warrant.

accounts.label: Raleigh dispatch in the Black press
accounts.gist: Three white men kidnapped several colored men after Bickett refused to return them on trivial charges, causing bitter feeling between the Carolinas.

framing.detail: Columbia dispatches treated it as the 'Mayfield kidnapping case', an extradition contest, stressing Mayfield's standing ('prominent planter', 'well-to-do') and calling the victims 'negro farm hands'.
Papers printed both sides' affidavits at length, and later headlines said the men 'Forcibly Arrested Negro Farm Hands ... Without Legal Process' and faced 'Serious Charges in Federal Court'.
The Chicago Whip ran it as 'Carolina Governors at Dagger Points', naming the abductors as white and stressing the 'tense and bitter feeling' between the states.
